claims.text: JR East's Shinkansen early warning can initiate braking before stronger earthquake shaking arrives; this is conditional, not guaranteed.
claims.scope: USGS supports the physics, not the identity of JR East's control system.

claims.text: Early warning detects an earthquake after it has started, rather than predicting one before it begins.
JR East's system detects preliminary P-wave tremors, which are the first seismic wave arrivals.
S waves and surface waves are slower and generally more damaging than the initial P waves.
Sensors detect earthquake motion and transmit warning information; the example is schematic, not a documented event.
claims.scope: The video gives a general illustrative sequence and does not claim JR uses the US processing architecture.

claims.text: When earthquake control requires it, cutting power to overhead wires is detected onboard and applies emergency braking.
claims.scope: No universal trigger threshold, brake delay or stopping distance is asserted.

claims.text: Telecommunications travel faster than seismic waves and can provide time for earlier protective action.
Near the earthquake focus, warning may not arrive before strong shaking; braking early is not a guarantee of a complete stop before shaking.
The useful mechanism is early detection and exploiting the time difference to reduce risk, rather than predicting earthquakes.

script.title: How Japan's Bullet Trains Get an Earthquake Head Start | Japan Explained
script.description: Why earthquake early warning can give JR East's Shinkansen trains a head start on braking, how P waves and faster communications make it possible, and why it cannot guarantee warning near the earthquake. #JapanExplained #Shorts

segments.text: Japan's bullet trains can begin braking before strong earthquake shaking arrives.
This is early warning, not prediction. The earthquake has already started.
J R East's system detects fast P waves, the first seismic vibrations.
Slower S waves and surface waves generally bring stronger shaking.
Imagine a sensor near the earthquake. It detects the first wave, then sends a warning toward the railway.
When the railway system decides action is needed, it cuts power, triggering the train's emergency brakes.
The electrical signal outruns seismic waves. That means braking can start while stronger shaking is still on its way.
But near the earthquake, the warning may arrive too late. Braking early does not guarantee stopping before shaking.
The takeaway: detect what has started, then use the time difference to reduce risk.
